questions.name: Alternate Ventilation and Advanced Airways
questions.keyword: advanced airway placed continuous compressions no pause
questions.text: AHA Part 8 explains what changes about CPR technique once an advanced airway is placed in an adult. Which statement matches?

answers.text: Compressions pause every 30 to allow 2 breaths, the same as before the airway
CPR stops entirely until the airway is confirmed secure
Compressions can be continuous without pausing for breaths
Ventilation rate doubles to 20 breaths per minute

explanations.a: Once an advanced airway is placed, there is no longer a need to pause compressions for breaths — one of the key benefits of advanced airway placement.
explanations.b: CPR does not stop after advanced airway placement; compressions and asynchronous breaths continue.
explanations.c: AHA Part 8 says that with an advanced airway in place, the Compressor can give continuous compressions without pausing for breaths.
explanations.d: Doubling the ventilation rate would hyperventilate the patient; the rate with an advanced airway is 10 per minute for adults.

questions.name: Alternate Ventilation and Advanced Airways
questions.keyword: advanced airway example endotracheal tube supraglottic
questions.text: AHA Part 8 lists examples of advanced airways. Which set matches?

answers.text: Nasopharyngeal airway and oral airway only
Only an endotracheal tube placed by a physician
Pocket mask and face shield only
Endotracheal tube and supraglottic airways

explanations.a: Nasopharyngeal and oral airways are basic airway adjuncts, not advanced airways.
explanations.b: Supraglottic devices can be placed by trained providers, not only physicians.
explanations.c: Pocket mask and face shield are barrier devices for breaths, not advanced airways.
explanations.d: AHA Part 8 lists the endotracheal tube and supraglottic airway devices as examples of advanced airways that require specialized training.

questions.name: Alternate Ventilation and Advanced Airways
questions.keyword: advanced airway specialized training required
questions.text: AHA Part 8 notes a key requirement for placing advanced airways during resuscitation. What is it?

answers.text: Advanced airways can be placed by any bystander without training
Advanced airways are only available in hospitals
Advanced airways are forbidden during CPR
Advanced airways require advanced training and are placed by trained providers

explanations.a: Advanced airway placement requires specific training; not every rescuer is qualified to place one.
explanations.b: Advanced airways are used both inside and outside hospitals when trained personnel are present.
explanations.c: Advanced airways improve airway management during prolonged resuscitation.
explanations.d: AHA Part 8 says placing advanced airways requires advanced training and is performed by trained health care professionals.

questions.name: Alternate Ventilation and Advanced Airways
questions.keyword: adult 1 breath every 6 seconds 10 per minute
questions.text: With an advanced airway in place during adult resuscitation, AHA specifies the ventilation rate as 1 breath every how many seconds?

answers.text: 1 breath every 6 seconds (10 per minute)
Pediatric rate: 1 breath every 2 to 3 seconds for children and infants
Provide no breaths; the advanced airway delivers oxygen passively
Deliver 1 breath every 3 minutes to avoid hyperventilation

explanations.a: AHA's high-quality CPR table specifies 1 breath every 6 seconds — 10 breaths per minute — for adults with an advanced airway.
explanations.b: The pediatric advanced-airway rate of 1 breath every 2 to 3 seconds is higher than the adult rate to match children's metabolic needs.
explanations.c: Advanced airways do not deliver oxygen passively; the Ventilator must actively squeeze the bag at the specified rate.
explanations.d: 1 breath every 3 minutes would be severely inadequate and would result in hypoxia.

questions.name: Alternate Ventilation and Advanced Airways
questions.keyword: peds 1 breath every 2 to 3 seconds advanced airway
questions.text: With an advanced airway in place during pediatric resuscitation, AHA specifies a different ventilation rate than for adults. How often should breaths be given?

answers.text: Adult advanced-airway rate: 1 breath every 6 seconds
No breaths after advanced airway placement
No breaths are needed because pediatric arrests are always cardiac
Deliver breaths only when the child shows cyanosis

explanations.a: 6 seconds between breaths is the adult rate; pediatric patients require faster ventilation.
explanations.b: Ventilations remain essential after advanced airway placement.
explanations.c: Pediatric arrests are primarily respiratory, so breaths are essential — not optional.
explanations.d: Waiting for visible cyanosis before ventilating would allow progressive hypoxia; breaths begin with the start of CPR.

questions.name: Alternate Ventilation and Advanced Airways
questions.keyword: hyperventilation avoid reduces cardiac output
questions.text: AHA Part 8 warns specifically about providing too many breaths during CPR with an advanced airway. Which consequence does the manual highlight?

answers.text: Excess ventilation increases cardiac output and improves survival
Too many breaths only affect blood pressure after ROSC
Extra breaths have no effect on circulation during CPR
Hyperventilation increases intrathoracic pressure, reduces venous return, and decreases cardiac output

explanations.a: Excess ventilation decreases, not increases, cardiac output.
explanations.b: The detrimental effect occurs during CPR itself, not only after ROSC.
explanations.c: Extra breaths measurably reduce CPR quality by increasing thoracic pressure.
explanations.d: AHA warns that hyperventilation during CPR increases intrathoracic pressure, impairs venous return to the heart, and decreases cardiac output during compressions.

questions.name: Alternate Ventilation and Advanced Airways
questions.keyword: too quickly forcefully volume causes gastric inflation
questions.text: AHA Part 8 identifies the primary causes of gastric inflation during ventilation. Which combination is correct?

answers.text: Using a pocket mask with a one-way valve
Performing head tilt-chin lift before each breath
Giving breaths too quickly, too forcefully, or with too much volume
Limiting each breath to 1 second

explanations.a: A pocket mask with a one-way valve is a recommended barrier device, not a cause of gastric inflation.
explanations.b: The head tilt-chin lift opens the airway and helps direct air into the lungs, reducing gastric inflation risk.
explanations.c: AHA Part 8 explicitly says giving breaths too quickly, too forcefully, or with too much volume causes air to enter the stomach.
explanations.d: One-second breaths are within AHA recommendations and are protective against gastric inflation.

questions.name: Alternate Ventilation and Advanced Airways
questions.keyword: gastric inflation serious complications regurgitation
questions.text: Why does AHA Part 8 caution rescuers about gastric inflation, beyond it being uncomfortable for the patient?

answers.text: Gastric inflation makes the AED unable to detect a rhythm
Gastric inflation always means the airway is fully obstructed
Gastric inflation prevents the rescuer from continuing compressions
Gastric inflation can result in regurgitation, aspiration, and other serious complications during resuscitation

explanations.a: AED detection is not affected by gastric inflation.
explanations.b: Gastric inflation does not equate to airway obstruction; air is reaching the stomach instead of the lungs.
explanations.c: Gastric inflation does not stop compressions, though it complicates the resuscitation.
explanations.d: AHA Part 8 warns that gastric inflation can lead to regurgitation, aspiration, and serious complications that worsen resuscitation outcomes.

questions.name: Alternate Ventilation and Advanced Airways
questions.keyword: even correct breaths gastric inflation may still occur
questions.text: AHA Part 8 makes an important qualification about gastric inflation during CPR. Which statement reflects the manual?

answers.text: Gastric inflation only occurs when breaths are given incorrectly
Gastric inflation does not occur during CPR, only after ROSC
Gastric inflation is completely preventable if the rescuer is trained
Gastric inflation can still develop even when breaths are given correctly during high-quality CPR

explanations.a: While incorrect technique increases the risk, correct technique does not fully eliminate it.
explanations.b: Gastric inflation occurs during CPR ventilations, not only after ROSC.
explanations.c: The manual explicitly acknowledges that correct technique cannot guarantee zero gastric inflation.
explanations.d: AHA Part 8 states that even if you give breaths correctly during high-quality CPR, gastric inflation may still develop.

questions.name: Alternate Ventilation and Advanced Airways
questions.keyword: reduce risk avoid too quickly too much volume
questions.text: To reduce the risk of gastric inflation during ventilation, AHA Part 8 recommends which approach?

answers.text: Avoid giving breaths too quickly, too forcefully, or with too much volume
Give breaths as rapidly as possible to minimize pause length
Skip breaths entirely to eliminate gastric inflation risk
Use maximum bag squeeze to ensure lung inflation

explanations.a: AHA Part 8 recommends avoiding breaths that are too quick, too forceful, or too voluminous to reduce the risk of gastric inflation.
explanations.b: Rapid breaths are one of the primary causes of gastric inflation.
explanations.c: Breaths remain essential during BLS; skipping them is not the AHA recommendation.
explanations.d: Maximum bag squeeze delivers excessive volume and worsens gastric inflation.

questions.name: Alternate Ventilation and Advanced Airways
questions.keyword: head tilt chin lift pinch nose seal lips 1 second
questions.text: AHA Part 8 describes mouth-to-mouth breathing for an adult when no barrier device is available. Which technique matches?

answers.text: Hold airway open with head tilt-chin lift, pinch the nose closed, take a regular breath, seal lips around the mouth, and give a 1-second breath that makes the chest rise
Take the deepest possible breath and exhale forcefully into the mouth
Press the patient's lips closed and blow into the nose only
Tilt the head down and blow under the chin

explanations.a: AHA Part 8 describes holding the airway open with head tilt-chin lift, pinching the nose, taking a regular breath, sealing lips around the mouth, and giving a 1-second breath that makes the chest rise.
explanations.b: Maximum-effort breaths cause hyperinflation and gastric inflation.
explanations.c: Mouth-to-nose is used only when mouth-to-mouth cannot be performed; the standard adult technique is mouth-to-mouth.
explanations.d: Tilting the head down closes the airway.

questions.name: Alternate Ventilation and Advanced Airways
questions.keyword: no chest rise repeat head tilt try again
questions.text: While giving mouth-to-mouth breaths to an adult, the first breath produces no chest rise. According to AHA Part 8, what should you do before the second breath?

answers.text: Press much harder on the second attempt
Skip the second breath and resume compressions
Repeat the head tilt-chin lift to reopen the airway, then try again
Insert a finger deep into the throat to feel for an obstruction

explanations.a: Pressing harder forces air into the stomach rather than the lungs.
explanations.b: Skipping the second breath abandons the 30:2 cycle.
explanations.c: AHA Part 8 directs the rescuer to repeat the head tilt-chin lift if the chest does not rise, then try again to give a breath that makes the chest rise.
explanations.d: Blind finger probing is contraindicated and may push an obstruction deeper.

questions.name: Alternate Ventilation and Advanced Airways
questions.keyword: regular breath not maximum volume just chest rise
questions.text: When giving mouth-to-mouth breaths, AHA Part 8 describes taking what kind of breath before sealing your lips around the patient's mouth?

answers.text: A deep maximum-capacity breath
A regular breath — normal volume, not maximum
Holding your own breath and blowing out residual air
No breath — blow while your own lungs are empty

explanations.a: A maximum-capacity breath delivers excessive volume and increases gastric inflation risk.
explanations.b: AHA Part 8 says take a regular breath before giving mouth-to-mouth, using only enough volume to make the chest rise.
explanations.c: Blowing out residual air would deliver hypoxic gas to the patient.
explanations.d: Blowing with empty lungs delivers no useful air volume.

questions.name: Alternate Ventilation and Advanced Airways
questions.keyword: no barrier device many settings public cardiac arrest
questions.text: AHA Part 8 notes that many cardiac arrests happen in settings where rescue equipment is not available. Which technique is described for these situations?

answers.text: Wait until a barrier device arrives before any ventilation
Skip ventilation entirely and only provide compressions
Use mouth-to-mouth or mouth-to-nose breaths when a barrier device is not available
Perform abdominal thrusts instead of breaths

explanations.a: Waiting for equipment delays critical ventilation; breaths without a barrier are acceptable.
explanations.b: While Hands-Only CPR is an option for untrained lay rescuers, trained providers should give breaths when possible.
explanations.c: AHA Part 8 describes mouth-to-mouth and mouth-to-nose as techniques for giving breaths when a barrier device is not available.
explanations.d: Abdominal thrusts are for choking, not for providing rescue breaths.

questions.name: Alternate Ventilation and Advanced Airways
questions.keyword: mouth to nose when mouth to mouth cannot be done
questions.text: AHA Part 8 describes mouth-to-nose breathing as an alternative. In which situation is it appropriate?

answers.text: It is always preferred over mouth-to-mouth for adults
When mouth-to-mouth breaths cannot be performed — for example, when the mouth cannot be opened
Only for children who cannot seal their lips
Only for infants, never adults

explanations.a: Mouth-to-mouth is the standard adult technique; mouth-to-nose is a fallback.
explanations.b: AHA Part 8 says mouth-to-nose breathing may be used when mouth-to-mouth cannot be performed — for example, if the person's mouth cannot be opened or the rescuer cannot make a good seal.
explanations.c: Children have their own age-appropriate technique; mouth-to-nose is an adult fallback, not exclusively for children.
explanations.d: Mouth-to-nose can be used for adults.

questions.name: Alternate Ventilation and Advanced Airways
questions.keyword: infant mouth and nose both covered small face
questions.text: AHA Part 8 describes a modification used when giving breaths to an infant without a barrier device. Which technique matches?

answers.text: Cover both the infant's mouth and nose with your mouth, then give a breath
Cover only the infant's nose and seal the mouth
Deliver breaths by blowing on the infant's forehead
An infant cannot receive mouth-to-mouth without a barrier

explanations.a: AHA Part 8 says for infants, you can cover both the mouth and nose with your mouth because of the infant's small face, and give breaths.
explanations.b: Covering only the nose while sealing the mouth is not the AHA infant breath technique.
explanations.c: Blowing on the forehead does not deliver air to the lungs.
explanations.d: Breaths can and should be given to an infant even without a barrier device if one is unavailable.

questions.name: Alternate Ventilation and Advanced Airways
questions.keyword: drowning mouth to nose cannot do mouth to mouth
questions.text: AHA Part 10 describes a drowning rescue scenario where mouth-to-mouth may not be feasible. Which alternative does the manual name?

answers.text: Skip rescue breaths entirely in all drowning cases
Use abdominal thrusts to expel water first, then attempt breaths
Mouth-to-nose breathing when mouth-to-mouth cannot be performed
Use a pocket mask only — never mouth-to-nose

explanations.a: Breaths are critical in drowning because arrests are primarily respiratory in cause.
explanations.b: AHA explicitly excludes abdominal thrusts as a water-removal technique.
explanations.c: AHA Part 10 says if for any reason you cannot give mouth-to-mouth breaths, give mouth-to-nose breaths instead.
explanations.d: AHA names mouth-to-nose as a legitimate alternative when mouth-to-mouth cannot be performed.

questions.name: Alternate Ventilation and Advanced Airways
questions.keyword: adult breathing support 1 breath every 5 to 6 seconds
questions.text: AHA Part 8 addresses ventilation for an adult who has a pulse but is not breathing adequately. How often should breaths be given?

answers.text: 1 breath every 5 to 6 seconds (10 to 12 per minute)
1 breath every 30 seconds
1 breath every 2 seconds (30 per minute)
Continuous breaths without pause

explanations.a: AHA Part 8 specifies 1 breath every 5 to 6 seconds (10 to 12 per minute) for an adult with a pulse who needs breathing support.
explanations.b: 1 breath every 30 seconds would be inadequate ventilation.
explanations.c: 1 breath every 2 seconds would be hyperventilation.
explanations.d: Continuous breaths without pausing would not allow exhalation or venous return.

questions.name: Alternate Ventilation and Advanced Airways
questions.keyword: pediatric breathing support 1 breath every 2 to 3 seconds
questions.text: AHA Part 8 specifies the breath rate for a child or infant with a pulse who is not breathing adequately. How often should breaths be given?

answers.text: 1 breath every 5 to 6 seconds
1 breath every 2 to 3 seconds (20 to 30 per minute)
1 breath every half-minute — grossly insufficient for a child
No breaths — observe only

explanations.a: 5 to 6 seconds is the adult rate; children and infants need a faster rate.
explanations.b: AHA Part 8 specifies 1 breath every 2 to 3 seconds for a child or infant with a pulse who needs breathing support.
explanations.c: 1 breath every 30 seconds is grossly inadequate for a child and would allow progressive hypoxia.
explanations.d: Observation without breaths would allow respiratory failure to progress to cardiac arrest.

questions.name: Alternate Ventilation and Advanced Airways
questions.keyword: assess pulse every 2 minutes during support
questions.text: While providing breaths to an adult with a pulse who is not breathing, AHA Part 8 directs the rescuer to monitor circulation. What is the recommended monitoring interval?

answers.text: Check for a pulse every 2 minutes
Check for a pulse once at the beginning only
Check for a pulse every 30 seconds
No pulse monitoring is needed during breath support

explanations.a: AHA Part 8 directs the rescuer to check for a pulse approximately every 2 minutes while providing breathing support.
explanations.b: A single pulse check at the start could miss a subsequent loss of pulse.
explanations.c: Checking every 30 seconds is unnecessarily frequent and interrupts breathing support.
explanations.d: Ongoing pulse monitoring is needed because the patient's condition may deteriorate.

questions.name: Alternate Ventilation and Advanced Airways
questions.keyword: if pulse absent start CPR
questions.text: AHA Part 8 instructs the rescuer providing breathing support to begin CPR if a specific finding occurs. What is that finding?

answers.text: If the patient begins to sweat
If no pulse is detected during the monitoring check
If two breaths fail to make the chest rise
If the patient's eyes close

explanations.a: Sweating is not the AHA-specified trigger for starting CPR during breath support.
explanations.b: AHA Part 8 says if no pulse is detected during the 2-minute monitoring check, immediately begin CPR.
explanations.c: Failed breaths prompt repositioning, not automatic CPR initiation; the pulse check is the trigger.
explanations.d: Eyes closing is not the AHA-specified trigger.

questions.name: Alternate Ventilation and Advanced Airways
questions.keyword: 2 rescuer bag mask better seal E-C clamp squeeze
questions.text: AHA Part 8 describes why 2-rescuer bag-mask technique is preferred over 1-rescuer technique. Which reason does the manual give?

answers.text: 2-rescuer technique uses less oxygen
One rescuer uses both hands to maintain a better mask seal while the other squeezes the bag, producing more effective ventilation
2-rescuer technique is faster because both rescuers can squeeze simultaneously
1-rescuer technique is always sufficient for adults

explanations.a: Oxygen consumption is not the AHA-cited reason for preferring 2-rescuer technique.
explanations.b: AHA Part 8 says 2-rescuer bag-mask technique is preferred because one rescuer uses both hands to maintain a better mask seal while the other squeezes the bag.
explanations.c: Both rescuers squeezing simultaneously delivers excessive volume.
explanations.d: While 1-rescuer technique can be performed, the 2-rescuer approach is specifically preferred for better seal quality.

questions.name: Alternate Ventilation and Advanced Airways
questions.keyword: connect supplemental oxygen when available
questions.text: AHA Part 8 addresses supplemental oxygen use with the bag-mask device. What does the manual instruct?

answers.text: Never connect supplemental oxygen during BLS
Connect the bag-mask device to supplemental oxygen when available
Connect oxygen only after ROSC is achieved
Wait for ALS authorization before using supplemental oxygen

explanations.a: Supplemental oxygen improves the quality of breaths delivered during resuscitation.
explanations.b: AHA Part 8 directs rescuers to connect the bag-mask device to supplemental oxygen when available.
explanations.c: Supplemental oxygen is most beneficial during ongoing resuscitation, not only after ROSC.
explanations.d: Supplemental oxygen use with bag-mask ventilation is within BLS scope.

questions.name: Alternate Ventilation and Advanced Airways
questions.keyword: bag mask size appropriate infant child cover mouth nose
questions.text: AHA Part 8 describes mask sizing for bag-mask ventilation in infants and children. Which criterion matches?

answers.text: The mask must cover only the nose for infants
The mask must be the same size as adult masks regardless of age
The mask must cover the mouth and nose without covering the eyes or extending below the chin
Mask size is irrelevant for bag-mask ventilation

explanations.a: The mask must cover both the mouth and nose, not only the nose.
explanations.b: Correctly sized pediatric masks are required; adult masks are not appropriate for small children.
explanations.c: AHA Part 8 specifies the mask must cover the infant's or child's mouth and nose completely without covering the eyes or extending below the bottom edge of the chin.
explanations.d: Mask size directly affects seal quality and ventilation effectiveness.
